explanations: Papyrus was made from the pith of Cyperus papyrus, a wetland sedge of the Nile Delta, in sheets joined and rolled into a scroll.
Parchment is made from the untanned skins of sheep, calves and goats, and by AD 400 had taken over from papyrus for works meant to last.
Paper is a thin sheet of matted cellulose fibres drained and dried from a pulp, a process developed in East Asia by 105 CE.
Papyrus, parchment and paper are three writing surfaces, in the order in which they took over from one another.

sources.excerpt: It was first known to have been used in Egypt (at least as far back as the First Dynasty), as the papyrus plant was once abundant across the Nile Delta. Papyrus was made from the pith of the papyrus plant, Cyperus papyrus, a wetland sedge.
Papyrus (plural: papyri or papyruses) can also refer to a document written on sheets of such material, joined side by side and rolled up into a scroll, an early form of a book.
Parchment is a writing material made from specially prepared untanned skins of animals—primarily sheep, calves and goats.
By 400 AD many of the written works intended for preservation in these regions had been transferred from papyrus to parchment.
Paper is a thin sheet of matted cellulose fibers.
Largely derived from lignocellulose, paper is created from a pulp dissolved into a slurry that is drained and dried into sheets.
The papermaking process developed in East Asia at least as early as 105 CE by the Han court eunuch Cai Lun, although archaeological evidence exists of 2nd century BCE paper-like material in China.
